title: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
summary: How 3DGS represents a scene as millions of anisotropic 3D Gaussians, projects them with EWA splatting, blends them with a sorting tile rasterizer, and fits them to photos with gradient descent and adaptive densification.
outcomes: Explain why rasterizing explicit Gaussians is far faster than NeRF's per-ray network queries
Compute a Gaussian's covariance from rotation and scales, and its 2D footprint via the projection Jacobian
Compute front-to-back alpha compositing of sorted splats at one pixel, including transmittance
Explain how the loss, clone, split, prune and opacity reset grow a scene from sparse SfM points
Estimate per-Gaussian memory and weigh 3DGS against NeRF-style methods

lessons.title: Why radiance fields needed a rasterizer instead of ray marching

blocks.md:
**Novel view synthesis** means: given photos of a static scene taken from known camera positions, render what a camera would see from a new position. A **radiance field** is the scene model behind most modern methods: a function that tells you, for any point in space, how dense it is and what color it emits toward a given direction.

Before 2023 the best-looking radiance fields were slow to train and very slow to render, and the fast ones looked worse. 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkuhler and Drettakis, SIGGRAPH 2023) was the first method to render unbounded real scenes at 1080p in real time (at least 30 frames per second) with quality on par with the best slow method.

To see why the earlier methods were slow, look at **NeRF** (Mildenhall et al., 2020). NeRF stores the scene inside a neural network: an MLP (8 fully connected ReLU layers, 256 channels each) that maps a 3D position and a viewing direction to a density $\sigma$ and a color $\mathbf{c}$.

To color one pixel, NeRF shoots a ray through it, picks sample points along the ray, queries the MLP at every sample, and blends the results with the volume rendering formula below. In the paper, each ray takes 64 samples for a coarse network and then 64 + 128 = 192 samples for a fine network.

blocks.caption: NeRF volume rendering along one ray. $\delta_i$ is the distance between samples; $T_i$ (transmittance) is how much light survives to sample $i$.

blocks.prompt: Using NeRF's sampling (64 coarse queries plus 192 fine queries per ray), roughly how many MLP evaluations does one 1920 x 1080 frame need?
blocks.reveal:
About **531 million**: $1920 \times 1080 = 2{,}073{,}600$ rays, times $64 + 192 = 256$ network queries per ray, is $530{,}841{,}600$ evaluations of an 8-layer MLP.

Most of those samples land in empty space or behind surfaces. NeRF training also needed 100k to 300k iterations, about 1 to 2 days on one V100 GPU. No amount of tuning makes this real time at 1080p; the representation itself has to change.

blocks.md:
The 3DGS paper points out that NeRF's formula is the same image formation model as **alpha blending** of sorted, semi-transparent points: if you write $\alpha_i = 1 - e^{-\sigma_i \delta_i}$, NeRF becomes $C = \sum_i \mathbf{c}_i \alpha_i \prod_{j<i}(1-\alpha_j)$. What differs is how you find the things to blend.

NeRF must *search* along every ray for where the matter is. 3DGS stores the matter *explicitly* as millions of small, colored, semi-transparent 3D Gaussian blobs. To render, it projects each blob onto the screen as a 2D ellipse (a **splat**) and blends the splats in depth order, the way a GPU rasterizer draws triangles. No neural network runs at render time.

blocks.title: The 3DGS pipeline: from photos to a trained splat scene

scenes.caption: Preprocessing: structure from motion (SfM) with COLMAP estimates each photo's camera pose and, as a side effect, a sparse 3D point cloud.
Each SfM point becomes one 3D Gaussian. Rendering projects every Gaussian to a 2D splat and a tile-based rasterizer blends the splats into an image.
Training compares the render with the real photo from the same camera. The rasterizer is differentiable, so gradients flow back to every Gaussian's parameters.
Every 100 iterations, adaptive density control adds Gaussians where the scene is under-covered and removes near-transparent ones, so the count grows from thousands to millions.

blocks.md:
The paper's headline numbers (Table 1, averaged over the Mip-NeRF360 dataset of 9 real scenes, rendered on an A6000 GPU) show both sides of the trade. **PSNR** (peak signal-to-noise ratio, in dB, higher is better) measures pixel accuracy against held-out test photos.

Mip-NeRF360, the quality leader at the time, trained for 48 hours and rendered at 0.06 FPS. 3DGS after 30,000 iterations reached 27.21 dB versus Mip-NeRF360's 27.69 dB while rendering at 134 FPS, after about 42 minutes of training. Its SSIM and LPIPS scores on that dataset were slightly better than Mip-NeRF360's.

blocks.title: Speed and quality on the Mip-NeRF360 scenes (paper Table 1)

scenes.caption: Render speed in frames per second. Mip-NeRF360's 0.06 FPS is too small to see; both 3DGS configurations exceed 130 FPS.
PSNR in dB on held-out views. Fast prior methods (Plenoxels, InstantNGP) trail; 3DGS at 30K iterations is within 0.5 dB of Mip-NeRF360.
Training time in minutes: 48 hours (2880 min) for Mip-NeRF360 versus about 6 and 42 minutes for 3DGS. Simplified: Mip-NeRF360 ran on 4 A100s for 12 hours, quoted as 48 GPU hours.

blocks.md: 3DGS keeps NeRF's blending formula but replaces the implicit neural field with explicit primitives. Explicit primitives can be projected and rasterized, so rendering cost scales with the number of splats that touch a pixel, not with hundreds of network queries per ray.

blocks.question: A colleague says 3DGS is fast because it uses a smaller neural network than NeRF. What is the more accurate explanation?
options: It uses a hash grid to make the MLP queries cheaper, like InstantNGP
It renders at lower resolution and upsamples the result
It has no network at render time: explicit Gaussians are projected and alpha blended by a sorting rasterizer
It skips the transmittance term, so each sample is independent
blocks.explain: 3DGS has no neural network at all. The scene is a list of Gaussians with stored parameters, and rendering is projection plus sorted alpha blending. The blending formula still includes transmittance; it is the same image formation model as NeRF.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Gaussian: position, covariance, opacity, SH color

blocks.md: Each primitive is a 3D Gaussian: a fuzzy ellipsoid whose influence falls off smoothly from its center. It is defined by a **mean** $\mu$ (the center position) and a $3 \times 3$ **covariance matrix** $\Sigma$ that sets its size, stretch and orientation. Its influence at a point $x$ is:

blocks.caption: Equal to 1 at the center and decaying in every direction. In rendering, $G$ is multiplied by the Gaussian's learned opacity to get its alpha.

blocks.md:
Why not just let gradient descent learn the 6 free numbers of the symmetric matrix $\Sigma$? A covariance matrix only means something if it is **positive semi-definite** (no negative variances along any axis). A raw gradient step can easily break that, and the Gaussian becomes invalid.

The paper instead stores two things that are always valid: a 3D **scale** vector $s$ and a **rotation** as a unit quaternion $q$ (4 numbers). It builds the scaling matrix $S = \mathrm{diag}(s)$ and the rotation matrix $R$ from $q$ (normalized first), and forms:

blocks.caption: Any $\Sigma$ built this way is valid by construction: it is $M M^{\top}$ with $M = RS$. Scales give the ellipsoid's axis lengths; $R$ turns the axes.

blocks.md: Let us see this in 2D on a small pixel grid (the same math with 2 axes). Take scales $s = (2, 0.75)$ pixels and a rotation of 30 degrees. Then $S S^{\top} = \mathrm{diag}(4, 0.5625)$ and

blocks.caption: Off-diagonal terms appear because the axes are tilted. The determinant stays $4 \times 0.5625 = 2.25$: rotation does not change the area.

blocks.title: One 2D Gaussian's footprint on a 7 x 7 pixel grid

scenes.caption: Isotropic Gaussian, scales (1.25, 1.25): a round blob. Cells show G at each pixel offset from the center (rows are y, columns are x).
Scales (2, 0.75), no rotation: stretched along x, thin along y. Same formula, different S.
Rotate by 30 degrees: the ellipse tilts. Pixel (x=2, y=1) now gets 0.53 while (x=1, y=2) gets only 0.17, because the long axis (tilted 30 degrees) points almost straight at (2, 1).
Multiply by opacity 0.8 to get alpha per pixel. Cells with alpha below 1/255 are masked: the official rasterizer skips them as invisible.

blocks.md: Two activation functions keep the stored numbers in a valid range while gradient descent moves them freely. Opacity is stored as a raw number passed through a **sigmoid**, so it stays in $[0, 1)$. Scales are stored as logs and passed through **exp**, so they stay positive. The quaternion is normalized before use. In the official code a new Gaussian starts with opacity 0.1.

Color is the last piece. Real surfaces look different from different angles (shine, reflections), so each Gaussian stores color as **spherical harmonics** (SH): a set of basis functions over directions, like a Fourier series on a sphere. Band $l$ has $2l+1$ functions, so degree 3 uses $1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16$ coefficients per color channel, or **48 numbers** for RGB.

At render time the rasterizer evaluates the SH in the direction from the camera to the Gaussian. Band 0 is the view-independent base color; in the official code that color is $0.5 + 0.2821 \times$ the band-0 coefficient (0.2821 is the constant SH basis value $1/(2\sqrt{\pi})$), and the result is clamped at 0.

scenes.caption: Geometry needs only 11 floats: 3 for the mean, 4 for the quaternion, 3 for the log-scales, 1 for opacity.
Band 0 adds the base RGB color: 3 floats. With only this, the Gaussian has the same color from every direction.
Bands 1 to 3 add 45 floats for view-dependent color. Total 59 floats, and 48 of them (81 percent) are color.

blocks.md: Opacity is not the alpha used in blending. Alpha at a pixel is opacity times the Gaussian's falloff $G$ at that pixel, so the same Gaussian contributes strongly at its center and almost nothing a few standard deviations away.

blocks.question: A teammate proposes storing each Gaussian's covariance as 6 free numbers (the upper triangle) and optimizing them directly with Adam. What is the main risk?
options: Gradient steps can produce a matrix that is not positive semi-definite, which is not a valid Gaussian
6 numbers cannot describe a rotated ellipsoid, so all Gaussians would be axis-aligned
Adam cannot optimize matrices, only vectors
It uses more memory than a quaternion plus a scale
blocks.explain: A symmetric 3 x 3 matrix has exactly 6 free numbers and can describe any ellipsoid, but nothing stops an update from making a variance negative. Factoring as $RSS^{\top}R^{\top}$ guarantees validity. It also uses 7 numbers, not fewer.

blocks.question: If you train with SH degree 1 instead of 3, how many floats does each Gaussian store?
blocks.explain: Degree 1 has $1 + 3 = 4$ coefficients per channel, so 12 color floats. Add 3 position, 4 rotation, 3 scale and 1 opacity: $12 + 11 = 23$.

lessons.title: Projecting Gaussians to splats and sorting them by tile

blocks.md: To draw a Gaussian, the renderer needs its 2D footprint on the screen. Perspective projection is not linear, so a projected Gaussian is not exactly a Gaussian. **EWA splatting** (Zwicker, Pfister, van Baar and Gross, 2001) solves this with a local linear approximation: around the Gaussian's center, replace the projection with its **Jacobian** $J$ (the matrix of first derivatives). With the camera's view transform $W$, the covariance in screen space is:

blocks.caption: Paper Eq. 5. Keep the top-left 2 x 2 block of $\Sigma'$: that is the splat's 2D covariance in pixels.

blocks.md: For a pinhole camera with focal length $f$ pixels, a point at camera coordinates $(t_x, t_y, t_z)$ lands at pixel $u = f t_x / t_z + c_x$. Differentiating gives the two rows of $J$ used by the official rasterizer:

blocks.tex: J = \begin{pmatrix} f/t_z & 0 & -f t_x / t_z^2 \\ 0 & f/t_z & -f t_y / t_z^2 \end{pmatrix}
blocks.caption: The $1/t_z$ factor shrinks far Gaussians; the last column accounts for off-center Gaussians being viewed at an angle.

blocks.md:
A worked example with real numbers. Take a 1280 x 720 image, $f = 800$, principal point $(640, 360)$, and the camera at the world origin so $W = I$. A Gaussian sits at $(0.4, -0.2, 4.0)$ meters with scales $(0.05, 0.02, 0.01)$ m, rotated 30 degrees about the view axis.

- Center pixel: $u = 800 \times 0.4/4 + 640 = 720$, $v = 800 \times (-0.2)/4 + 360 = 320$.
- $J$ has $f/t_z = 200$, and last-column entries $-20$ and $10$.
- The 2D covariance comes out as $\begin{pmatrix}79.04 & 36.35\\ 36.35 & 37.01\end{pmatrix}$ square pixels.

The official code then adds 0.3 to both diagonal entries, a small low-pass filter so every splat is at least about one pixel wide (79.34 and 37.31 here). The larger eigenvalue of the result is 100.3, so the standard deviation along the long axis is about 10 pixels.

The rasterizer bounds each splat by a radius of 3 standard deviations, rounded up: $\lceil 3\sqrt{100.3}\rceil = 31$ pixels. That box spans pixels 689 to 751 in x and 289 to 351 in y.

Now the **tile-based rasterizer**. The screen is cut into 16 x 16 pixel tiles; a 1280 x 720 image has $80 \times 45 = 3600$ tiles. Our splat's box touches tile columns 43 to 46 and tile rows 18 to 21, so it overlaps 16 tiles.

The renderer first culls Gaussians whose 99 percent confidence region misses the view frustum. Then it makes one copy (an *instance*) of each Gaussian per tile it overlaps and gives each instance a 64-bit sort key: the **tile ID in the high bits**, the **view-space depth in the low 32 bits**. One GPU radix sort over all keys groups instances by tile *and* orders each tile front to back, all at once.

blocks.title: Duplicate, key, sort: building per-tile lists

scenes.caption: Four Gaussians over three tiles. A overlaps tiles 0 and 1, C overlaps tiles 1 and 2, so each gets two instances. Six instances, in Gaussian order.
Key = (tile ID, depth). After one radix sort the instances are grouped by tile, and within tile 1 the order is C (1.0 m), A (2.0 m), B (5.0 m): front to back.
One thread per entry compares its tile ID with its neighbors to find where each tile's range starts and ends. Tile 1 owns entries 1 to 3.
Rasterization: one GPU thread block per tile, one thread per pixel. The block loads its tile's sorted splats into shared memory in batches and every pixel blends them front to back.

blocks.md: The sort is per tile, by each Gaussian's center depth, not per pixel. Where two large splats interpenetrate, the true order can differ from pixel to pixel, so blending is approximate. The paper notes this error becomes negligible as splats shrink toward pixel size, and lists sudden order switches (popping) as a limitation.
Duplicating each Gaussian once per tile raises the work somewhat, but it turns rendering into a sort plus fully parallel, branch-light loops, which is what GPUs do best.

blocks.question: A Gaussian moves twice as far from the camera along the view axis (all else equal, centered on screen). What happens to its 2D covariance entries?
options: They halve, because $J$ scales with $1/t_z$
They stay the same, because the 3D covariance did not change
They double, because the Gaussian is farther away
They drop to a quarter, because $J$ appears twice in $J W \Sigma W^{\top} J^{\top}$
blocks.explain: For a centered Gaussian, $J$ is roughly $(f/t_z) I$ on x and y. The covariance is sandwiched between $J$ and $J^{\top}$, so it scales by $(f/t_z)^2$: doubling the distance quarters the variance and halves the radius in pixels, as perspective should.

blocks.question: Why does the sort key put the tile ID in the high bits and the depth in the low bits, rather than the reverse?
options: So a single sort groups instances by tile first, and orders each tile's instances by depth
Because depth needs more than 32 bits of precision
So that far Gaussians are drawn first, as in the painter's algorithm
Because radix sort only looks at the low 32 bits
blocks.explain: Sorting by a combined key orders by its high bits first. With tile ID on top, all instances of a tile become contiguous, and ties within a tile are broken by depth, giving a front-to-back list per tile from one global sort.

lessons.title: Alpha compositing sorted splats at one pixel

blocks.md: Inside a tile, each pixel walks its sorted list of splats from front to back. For splat $i$ it computes the splat's alpha at that pixel, $\alpha_i = \min(0.99,\ o_i\,G_i(\text{pixel}))$, where $o_i$ is the learned opacity and $G_i$ the 2D Gaussian falloff. The pixel color is:

blocks.caption: Paper Eq. 3. The product is the transmittance $T_i$: the fraction of light not yet absorbed by the splats in front of splat $i$.

blocks.md:
Work it at one pixel with 4 splats already sorted front to back. Opacities are $0.9, 0.7, 0.95, 0.6$ and the falloffs at this pixel are $0.5, 0.8, 0.6, 0.9$, giving alphas $0.45, 0.56, 0.57, 0.54$. We track only the red channel; the splats' red values are $0.9, 0.2, 0.5, 0.1$, and the background is black.

Each step does three things: weight = $\alpha_i T$, add weight times color to $C$, then shrink $T$ by $(1-\alpha_i)$.

blocks.title: Front-to-back alpha compositing at one pixel

scenes.caption: Start with transmittance T = 1 (nothing blocks the view yet) and C = 0.
Splat 1 has a larger alpha (0.56) but only 55 percent of the light reaches it: weight 0.308, C = 0.467.
Splat 2: T = 0.242, weight 0.138, C = 0.536. Each later splat matters less because the ones in front absorb light.
Splat 3: T = 0.104, weight 0.056, final C = 0.541. Remaining T = 0.048 lets 4.8 percent of the black background through.

blocks.prompt: Suppose a bug sorts this tile back to front, so the same formula processes the splats in order 3, 2, 1, 0. What red value does the pixel get instead of 0.541?
blocks.reveal:
**0.243**, less than half. Now splat 3 (red 0.1, alpha 0.54) is treated as the front surface and takes weight 0.54, while the bright splat 0 (red 0.9) is pushed to the back with weight about 0.039.

The four weights still sum to the same $1 - T = 0.952$ either way, because the product of $(1-\alpha_i)$ does not depend on order. Only *who* gets the weight changes, which is why the rasterizer must sort.

blocks.title: The per-pixel blend loop (simplified from the official CUDA kernel)
blocks.code:
T = 1.0
C = 0.0
for i in sorted_splats_front_to_back:
    alpha = min(0.99, opacity[i] * G[i])
    if alpha < 1/255:
        continue            # invisible, skip
    test_T = T * (1 - alpha)
    if test_T < 0.0001:
        break               # pixel is saturated
    C += color[i] * alpha * T
    T = test_T
out = C + T * background

scenes.caption: Initial state for one pixel.
Splat 0: alpha 0.45 passes the 1/255 check and test_T = 0.55 is well above 0.0001, so it blends.
Splats 1 and 2 blend the same way.
Splat 3 is the last in the list. The loop ends with T = 0.0479 and the background (black) adds nothing.
Early stopping: if a pixel's T would drop below 0.0001 the thread stops, and the whole tile stops once all its pixels are saturated. Opaque surfaces stop after a few splats.

blocks.md:
Training needs the gradient of this loop. Most earlier point renderers stored per-pixel lists of blended points, or capped how many points per pixel receive gradients. 3DGS does neither. The backward pass re-walks the same sorted tile lists **back to front**, and recovers each intermediate transmittance by starting from the final $T$ saved in the forward pass and dividing by $(1-\alpha_i)$ step by step. That is constant extra memory per pixel.

The $\alpha \le 0.99$ clamp and the 1/255 skip exist partly to keep those divisions numerically stable.
Pixel color is a weighted sum of splat colors with weights $\alpha_i T_i$. Order changes who gets the weight, and every splat with nonzero weight receives a gradient.

blocks.question: The paper's ablation limits gradients to the 10 front-most splats per pixel (a Pulsar-style shortcut). What did they observe?
options: No visible change, because splats beyond the 10th have negligible weight
Unstable optimization; on the Truck scene PSNR dropped by about 11 dB
Training became 10 times faster with a small quality loss
Only the background degraded, because it is the farthest away
blocks.explain: Table 3 (Limited-BW) shows a severe drop: about 11 dB on Truck and an average of 19.19 dB versus 26.05 dB for the full method at 30K iterations. Splats behind the first 10 still carry weight during training, when many are semi-transparent.

lessons.title: Training: the loss, clone, split, prune and opacity reset

blocks.md:
Training starts from the camera calibration. The paper takes photos and runs **COLMAP**, a structure-from-motion (SfM) system: it detects and matches features across images, then jointly solves for every camera's pose and the 3D positions of the matched features. The 3DGS repository's `convert.py` runs COLMAP's `feature_extractor`, `exhaustive_matcher`, `mapper` and `image_undistorter` for this.

Each sparse SfM point becomes a Gaussian: its position is the point, its color comes from the point's color, it starts isotropic with a radius equal to the mean distance to its 3 nearest neighbors, and (in the code) opacity 0.1.

Then the loop from the prerequisite course runs: render a training view, compare it with the photo, backpropagate, update. The official code uses Adam with a separate learning rate per parameter group; the position learning rate decays exponentially from 0.00016 to 0.0000016 (scaled by the scene size) over 30,000 iterations. The loss mixes a per-pixel error with a structural one:

blocks.caption: Paper Eq. 7. $\mathcal{L}_1$ is the mean absolute pixel difference. The official code computes the D-SSIM term as $1 - \text{SSIM}$.

blocks.md:
**SSIM** (structural similarity) compares local means, variances and correlations in small windows, so it rewards matching edges and texture rather than only average color. Example: a render with mean absolute error $\mathcal{L}_1 = 0.05$ and SSIM $0.85$ gives $\mathcal{L} = 0.8 \times 0.05 + 0.2 \times 0.15 = 0.04 + 0.03 = 0.07$.

The slider plot shows the loss as a function of $\lambda$ for given L1 and SSIM values; the paper fixes $\lambda = 0.2$ for every scene.

blocks.title: How lambda mixes L1 and D-SSIM

scenes.caption: With L1 = 0.05 and SSIM = 0.85, the loss at lambda 0.2 is 0.07: 0.04 from L1 and 0.03 from D-SSIM.
A blurry render can have small L1 but poor SSIM (0.70). The D-SSIM term now dominates even at lambda 0.2, pushing the optimizer toward sharp detail.
A color shift raises L1 (0.15) while structure stays good (SSIM 0.95): the L1 term carries the signal.

blocks.md:
The SfM points are too sparse to describe a full scene, so the optimizer must be able to create Gaussians. **Adaptive density control** runs every 100 iterations from iteration 500 to 15,000 in the official code. It looks at each Gaussian's average view-space position gradient. A large gradient means the optimizer keeps trying to move the Gaussian, a sign that the region is not well reconstructed. Gaussians above the threshold $\tau_{\text{pos}} = 0.0002$ are densified in one of two ways:

- **Clone** (under-reconstruction): a small Gaussian is copied, and the copy is moved along the positional gradient to cover missing geometry (the official code places the copy at the original's position and lets optimization separate them). Total volume grows.
- **Split** (over-reconstruction): a large Gaussian covering detail it cannot represent is replaced by two, with scales divided by $\phi = 1.6$ and positions sampled from the original Gaussian as a probability distribution. Total volume stays about the same.

blocks.title: One refinement step for one Gaussian

scenes.caption: Pruning: Gaussians that are nearly transparent, or very large in world space or on screen, are removed (thresholds from the official code).
Densification starts from the positional gradient, averaged over the views since the last step. Below 0.0002, the Gaussian is left alone.
A small Gaussian with a large gradient sits where geometry is missing: clone it.
A large Gaussian with a large gradient is smearing over detail: split it into two smaller ones.

blocks.md: Floaters (blobs hanging in front of the cameras) can make the count explode. Every 3000 iterations the paper resets all opacities to near zero. Gaussians that matter regain opacity through gradients; the rest stay transparent and get pruned. Two more stabilizers: training starts at 4 times lower image resolution, upsampled twice (after 250 and 500 iterations), and SH bands are switched on one at a time every 1000 iterations, since early view-dependent color can produce wrong base colors.

blocks.title: The default 30,000-iteration schedule (paper and official code)

scenes.caption: The paper warms up at a quarter of the resolution and upsamples twice, after 250 and 500 iterations (the official code skips this and trains at one resolution). Only SH band 0 (base color) is trained at first.
An SH band is added every 1000 iterations until degree 3 at iteration 3000.
Clone, split and prune every 100 iterations from 500 to 15,000; opacity resets every 3000. After 15,000 the set of Gaussians is fixed and only their parameters keep improving.

blocks.md: Densification is driven by the *positional* gradient, not by the photometric error at a pixel directly. A region can look wrong yet not densify if its Gaussians are not being pushed around, which is one reason poorly observed regions stay blurry.

blocks.question: During training a thin railing is rendered as one long, blurry Gaussian with a large positional gradient. Its largest scale is 5 percent of the scene extent. What does the default density control do?
options: Clone it, because large gradients always mean missing geometry
Prune it, because its gradient is large
Reset its opacity to zero right away
Split it into two Gaussians with scales divided by 1.6
blocks.explain: The gradient passes the 0.0002 threshold, and the Gaussian is larger than 1 percent of the scene extent, so it counts as over-reconstruction: split. Cloning is for small Gaussians; pruning depends on opacity and size, not gradient.

blocks.question: Why do periodic opacity resets reduce the number of Gaussians?
options: They delete every Gaussian whose opacity is below 0.5
After the reset, only Gaussians the loss actually needs regain opacity; the rest stay near zero and fall under the pruning threshold
They shrink all scales, which merges neighboring Gaussians
They disable densification for the next 3000 iterations
blocks.explain: Setting opacity near zero is a test: Gaussians that help explain the photos get their opacity pushed back up by gradients, while floaters and redundant ones do not, and then get pruned for being nearly transparent.

lessons.title: Memory cost, ablations, failure modes and gsplat in practice

blocks.md:
The price of explicit primitives is memory. Each Gaussian stores 59 float32 values, or **236 bytes**. The paper reports 1 to 5 million Gaussians for the scenes it tested. At 3 million Gaussians:

- $3{,}000{,}000 \times 236 = 708{,}000{,}000$ bytes, about **708 MB** (675 MiB).
- With SH degree 0 only (14 floats each) it would be 168 MB, losing view-dependent effects.

This matches the scale in Table 1: 734 MB on average for 3DGS-30K on the Mip-NeRF360 scenes, versus 8.6 MB for Mip-NeRF360's network weights. During training of large scenes the paper reports peak GPU memory above 20 GB for its unoptimized prototype.

blocks.caption: Per-Gaussian storage at SH degree 3. Color dominates, which is why compression work often targets SH coefficients.

blocks.md: Which design choices actually matter? The paper's ablation (Table 3) trains three scenes (Truck, Garden, Bicycle) with one component removed at a time. Average PSNR at 30K iterations:

blocks.title: Ablations: average PSNR at 30K iterations (paper Table 3)

scenes.caption: The full method averages 26.05 dB over Truck, Garden and Bicycle.
Removing cloning, SH, or anisotropy (one scalar radius per Gaussian) each costs about 0.1 to 0.9 dB on average.
Large losses: no splitting (23.90), random instead of SfM initialization (20.42), and limiting gradients to 10 splats per pixel (19.19).

blocks.md:
Failure modes the paper itself reports:

- **Poorly observed regions** show artifacts, including elongated or splotchy Gaussians; other methods struggle there too.
- **Popping**: large Gaussians can suddenly switch depth order, or be rejected by the rasterizer's guard band near the camera. Anti-aliasing and better culling are left as future work.
- **Floaters**: blobs close to the input cameras; the opacity reset and size-based pruning control them.
- **No regularization**: the optimization only matches photos, so geometry is not guaranteed to be a clean surface. Very large scenes may need a lower position learning rate.

In practice, many projects use **gsplat** (Nerfstudio team), an open-source library with PyTorch bindings and CUDA kernels. Its paper reports up to 10 percent less training time and 4 times less memory than the original implementation. Its `rasterization` function takes the parameters from this course directly: means, quaternions, scales, opacities, and colors or SH coefficients, plus camera view matrices and intrinsics. Densification is packaged as strategies such as `DefaultStrategy` (the paper's clone, split, prune) and `MCMCStrategy`.

blocks.code:
import torch
from gsplat import rasterization

N = 100_000
means = torch.randn(N, 3, device="cuda")              # mu
quats = torch.randn(N, 4, device="cuda")              # normalized inside
scales = torch.rand(N, 3, device="cuda") * 0.02       # after exp
opacities = torch.rand(N, device="cuda")               # after sigmoid
sh = torch.randn(N, 16, 3, device="cuda")              # degree 3: 16 coeffs x RGB

viewmats = torch.eye(4, device="cuda")[None]           # [C, 4, 4] world to camera
Ks = torch.tensor([[800., 0, 640], [0, 800., 360], [0, 0, 1]], device="cuda")[None]

colors, alphas, meta = rasterization(

blocks.md: 3DGS trades memory for speed: hundreds of megabytes of explicit parameters instead of a few megabytes of network weights, in exchange for rendering at well over 30 FPS and training in tens of minutes.

blocks.question: You need to stream a 3DGS scene to phones and your budget is tight. Which change cuts the most storage per Gaussian while keeping geometry intact?
options: Drop the quaternion and use isotropic Gaussians
Store opacity in 8 bits instead of 32
Reduce SH degree from 3 to 0 or 1, giving up some view-dependent color
Remove the position and infer it from the sort order
blocks.explain: 48 of the 59 floats are SH color. Dropping to degree 0 keeps 14 floats (168 MB instead of 708 MB at 3 million Gaussians). Isotropic Gaussians save only 6 floats and hurt geometry; the paper's ablation shows anisotropy matters.

blocks.question: Compared with Mip-NeRF360, which statement about 3DGS (30K iterations) on the Mip-NeRF360 dataset matches the paper?
options: Higher PSNR, faster training, and a smaller model
Slightly lower PSNR, much faster training and rendering, and a much larger model
Same PSNR and same model size, but faster rendering
Lower quality on every metric, but real-time rendering
blocks.explain: Table 1: PSNR 27.21 vs 27.69 dB (slightly lower), but SSIM and LPIPS slightly better, training about 42 minutes vs 48 hours, 134 vs 0.06 FPS, and 734 MB vs 8.6 MB.
